title: If You Want Outsiders to Invest, Ask for Their Advice, Not Their Money
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article addresses the discomfort of asking outsiders for financial or time commitments, noting that most people instinctively guard their resources and slow-walk direct requests. The counterintuitive fix offered is to reframe the ask: request advice and counsel about a project instead of money or time outright. Because advice-seeking doesn't trigger the same defensiveness as a direct financial pitch, it opens a more honest, engaged conversation about the initiative's merits. The author notes that even when the advice-seeking conversation doesn't convert to investment, it often produces valuable direction or referrals to other prospects.
points: Direct requests for money or time trigger defensiveness because people protect scarce resources by default.
Reframing the ask as a request for advice and counsel lowers people's guard and opens a more genuine conversation.
This approach lets both sides explore the real merits of a project without the pressure of an immediate financial decision.
Even when a specific ask doesn't convert into investment, the advice-seeking approach often yields useful direction or referrals.
quotes: Those on the receiving end of these requests are naturally suspicious as to what the ask involves.
We can summarize the wisdom like this: Ask for money and time from people, and you will most often get advice and counsel about your project.
Ask for advice and counsel about your initiative, and you will often receive money and time.
Because they are being asked for their wise counsel, and not for an investment, they let down their guard and engage with an open mind.
Even when the investment does not materialize, the advice and direction leaders often receive is of tremendous value.
You might find the power of a fully engaged conversation about the possibilities produces more results than the direct assault of asking for an investment.
